readiness.definition: Patient has no current intention to quit smoking within the next 6 months; may be unaware or under-aware of the need to change.
Patient is seriously considering quitting within the next 6 months but has not yet committed to action.
Patient intends to quit within the next 30 days and may have already taken small preparatory steps (e.g. cutting back, setting a quit date).
Patient has actively quit smoking within the last 6 months and is practicing new behaviors.
Patient has been smoke-free for more than 6 months and is working to prevent relapse.
Patient had previously quit but has resumed smoking and may be cycling back to an earlier stage.

concern.definition: Concerns about physical health symptoms or bodily effects of smoking or quitting.
Concerns about emotional or mental wellbeing tied to smoking or quitting.
Concerns about the cost of smoking/cessation aids, social stigma, or impact on family/relationships.
Concerns tied to specific contexts or situations that put the patient at risk of relapse.

trigger.definition: Work, financial, or personal stress that the patient directly links to smoking urges or behavior.
Social settings or interactions (e.g. being around other smokers, social gatherings) that the patient links to smoking urges.
Routine or habitual cues (e.g. morning coffee, after meals, driving) that the patient links to smoking behavior.

NOT a trigger — motivations to quit, health/financial/family concerns, consequences of smoking, or future goals must not be classified as triggers unless the patient explicitly links them to smoking urges or behavior.

attempt.definition: Abrupt, unaided cessation without medication or behavioral support.
Nicotine Replacement Therapy — patches, gum, lozenges, inhalers, or nasal spray.
Prescription cessation medication such as varenicline (Chantix) or bupropion (Zyban).
Counseling, support groups, quitlines, or structured behavioral programs.

advice.definition: Counselor recommends nicotine replacement therapy (patch, gum, lozenge, inhaler).
Counselor recommends behavioral strategies (stress management, coping plans, routine changes).
Counselor refers the patient to another specialist or resource (e.g. nutritionist, support group, quitline).
Counselor and patient agree on a concrete quit date or scheduling commitment.
